title: Complexity Analysis and Asymptotics
relevance: Interviewers and OAs use asymptotic complexity to judge whether a solution will scale under constraints, independent of machine speed or language.

phases.goal: Establish why complexity analysis exists and how Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta formally bound growth.

must_hit.point: Wall-clock timing is flawed because runtime depends on hardware, language, compiler optimizations, and system load.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects seconds-based timing and names machine/environment dependence as the reason.

must_hit.point: Complexity counts fundamental operations as a function of input size n, so performance can be compared as n grows toward infinity.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says we measure operation counts vs n, not seconds, to study scaling.

must_hit.point: Asymptotic notation keeps the dominant term and drops constants and lower-order terms for large n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains we ignore constants/lower-order terms and focus on the leading growth term.

must_hit.point: f(n) is O(g(n)) if positive constants c and n0 exist such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0 (upper/worst-case bound).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the inequality form or clearly says asymptotic upper bound with c and n0.

must_hit.point: f(n) is Ω(g(n)) with f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for n ≥ n0; Θ means both O and Ω, sandwiching f between c1·g and c2·g.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes lower bound Ω from tight Θ as both O and Ω.

must_hit.point: In interviews people often say O(n) when they mean Θ(n); standard interview convention still uses O for upper bounds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate notes colloquial O vs mathematical Θ and that interviews stick to O as upper-bound convention.

probes: Why don't we just time an algorithm in seconds to decide if it's efficient?
Formally, what does it mean for f(n) to be O(g(n))?
How do Big-Omega and Big-Theta relate to Big-O?

hints.1: Think about what changes if you run the same code on different machines or languages.
hints.2: Complexity tracks operation count vs n; asymptotic notation keeps the dominant term and uses O/Ω/Θ bounds.
hints.3: O: f ≤ c·g past n0 (upper); Ω: f ≥ c·g (lower); Θ: both, so c1·g ≤ f ≤ c2·g; interviews still say O for upper bounds.

phases.goal: Apply case analysis, common classes, amortized cost, space (including recursion), and the Master Theorem.

must_hit.point: Best/worst/average cases depend on input values: for linear search, best is O(1) (target first), worst O(n) (last or missing), average O(n) after dropping the 1/2 from about n/2 checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives all three linear-search cases and notes average still O(n) after dropping the constant.

must_hit.point: QuickSort worst case is O(n²) with consistently bad pivots; average with a random pivot is O(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts QuickSort O(n²) worst vs O(n log n) average under random pivot.

must_hit.point: Common classes from fastest to slowest include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ), O(n!); e.g. log₂(n)≈20 when n=10⁶, quadratic feasible for n≤5000, exponential unusable beyond n≈25, factorial beyond n≈12.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate orders major classes and can cite at least one growth/feasibility fact from the hierarchy.

must_hit.point: Amortized analysis averages cost over a worst-case sequence: vector push_back is O(n) on reallocation but aggregate cost of n pushes is O(n), so amortized push_back is O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains rare doubling copies vs many cheap inserts and concludes amortized O(1) per push_back.

must_hit.point: Interview 'space complexity' almost always means auxiliary space (extra memory excluding input); recursion depth n for printDown means O(n) auxiliary space via the call stack.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates total vs auxiliary space and counts recursive stack frames as memory.

must_hit.point: Master Theorem for T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) with f(n)=O(nᵈ): Case1 a>bᵈ → O(n^{log_b a}); Case2 a=bᵈ → O(nᵈ log n); Case3 a<bᵈ → O(nᵈ). Merge sort (a=2,b=2,d=1) and binary search (a=1,b=2,d=0) are both Case 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the three cases and correctly places merge sort as O(n log n) and binary search as O(log n) via Case 2.

probes: For linear search, what are best, worst, and average-case complexities?
Why can std::vector::push_back be amortized O(1) if a single push can take O(n)?
Using the Master Theorem, what is the complexity of merge sort?

hints.1: Walk a concrete example: searching an array, or pushing into a growing vector.
hints.2: Cases depend on input values; amortized averages a worst-case sequence; Master Theorem compares a to bᵈ.
hints.3: Linear search: O(1)/O(n)/O(n); n pushes cost O(n) total so amortized O(1); merge sort a=bᵈ=2 → O(n log n).

phases.goal: Clarify when worst-case, amortized, auxiliary space, and tight vs loose bounds are the right lens.

must_hit.point: Worst-case single-operation analysis can be too pessimistic for sequences; amortized analysis is appropriate when rare expensive ops are paid for by many cheap ones.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says when to prefer amortized over per-op worst case, citing dynamic array growth.

must_hit.point: Total space includes input plus extra; auxiliary space excludes input—interviews almost always want auxiliary.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate clearly picks auxiliary when asked for space in an interview and explains why.

must_hit.point: Worst case gives a guarantee and is usually what we care about most; average case needs an assumed distribution (often uniform).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains worst-case as a guarantee and that average case assumes a probability model.

probes: When would you report amortized complexity instead of worst-case per operation?
If an interviewer asks for space complexity, do they mean total or auxiliary space?

hints.1: Think about data structures where most operations are cheap but occasional ones are costly.
hints.2: Compare a single expensive reallocation vs cost averaged over a long sequence; also total vs extra memory.
hints.3: Use amortized for sequence-average (e.g. vector growth); in interviews 'space' nearly always means auxiliary, not including the input.

phases.goal: Map constraints to feasible complexities and avoid hidden library costs when stating time and space.

must_hit.point: Modern servers comfortably do around 10⁸ simple C++ ops per second; with a 1-second limit, reverse-engineer target complexity from max n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites ~10⁸ ops/sec and uses n's magnitude to pick a complexity class.

must_hit.point: Constraint map: n≤10..12 → n!/2ⁿ; n≤20..25 → 2ⁿ; n≤500 → n³; n≤5000 → n²; n≤10⁵..10⁶ → n log n or n; n≥10⁷..10⁸ → n or log n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps at least two constraint bands to the matching target complexity/technique.

must_hit.point: For n≤10⁵, an O(n²) nested-loop solution needs 10¹⁰ operations and will TLE; need O(n log n) or O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate flags O(n²) under n≤10⁵ as TLE and names the needed tighter bound.

must_hit.point: Hidden costs: string concatenation s=s+"a" is O(k) in current length (loop → O(n²)); map ops are O(log n) so n lookups are O(n log n); substr copies in O(L).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names at least one library pitfall and the resulting tighter/worse complexity.

must_hit.point: When stating complexity, give both time and auxiliary space with a one-sentence justification each.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate pairs time and space with brief justifications (e.g. sort + hashmap frequencies).

probes: If an OA has n ≤ 10⁵, why is a nested O(n²) loop likely to fail?
What hidden complexity costs should you watch for with string concatenation or std::map inside a loop?
How should you present time and space complexity in an interview answer?

hints.1: Estimate how many operations your approach performs at the maximum n.
hints.2: Use the ~10⁸ ops/sec rule and the constraint→complexity table; also cost library calls inside loops.
hints.3: n≤10⁵ forbids O(n²) (~10¹⁰ ops); map in a loop is O(n log n); state time and auxiliary space with a short why.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Timing in seconds mixes hardware, language, compiler, and load; complexity counts operations vs n so algorithms can be compared by growth as n → ∞.

tradeoffs.topic: Worst-case per operation vs amortized analysis
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Per-op worst case for vector push_back is O(n) on resize, but over a worst-case sequence of n pushes aggregate cost is O(n), so amortized cost per push is O(1).
Total space includes the input; auxiliary is extra temporary memory excluding input. Interview 'space complexity' almost always means auxiliary, including recursion stack frames.
Θ is the tight bound (both O and Ω). Industry/interviews often say O(n) when they mean Θ(n), but interview convention still uses O for upper bounds.
Worst case is the maximum ops for size n and usually what we care about as a guarantee; average case is expected ops under an assumed distribution (often uniform).

gotchas.trap: Ignoring that recursion uses memory even with no dynamic allocation
gotchas.correction: Each call adds a stack frame; printDown recursing n times has maximum stack depth n, so auxiliary space is O(n).

gotchas.trap: Treating std::string concatenation, std::map operations, or .substr() as O(1) inside loops
gotchas.correction: s=s+"a" is O(k) in current length (n concatenations → O(n²)); map insert/lookup is O(log n) (n ops → O(n log n)); .substr() copies in O(L).

gotchas.trap: Submitting O(n²) for n ≤ 10⁵ because it 'looks simple'
gotchas.correction: That is about 10¹⁰ operations vs ~10⁸ per second in C++, so TLE; need O(n log n) or O(n).

gotchas.trap: Reporting only time complexity, or conflating amortized O(1) with every single operation being O(1)
gotchas.correction: State time and auxiliary space with a one-line justification; amortized O(1) means the average over a long sequence is bounded by a constant even if occasional ops are expensive.
